11. Calculating Slider Handle Position and Width

The slider handles that adjust the start/end of an edit section (playable section) need to show their clipped portion even when the section only partially overlaps the visible screen. So instead of clamping position/width to 0 and range(), they're clamped to a range padded by the handle's own width.

private syncSliderCoordinates(playableSection: VideoEditor.PlayableSection): void {
  const {startTimeSec, endTimeSec} = playableSection;

  const xPos = this.sidePadding() + startTimeSec * this.pixelPerSecond() - this.baseCoordinatesX();
  const sectionDuration = endTimeSec - startTimeSec;
  const sectionDurationWidth = sectionDuration * this.pixelPerSecond();
  const sliderLeft = Math.max(-this.HANDLE_WIDTH, Math.min(xPos, this.range() + this.HANDLE_WIDTH));
  // Use the handle width instead of 0 as the boundary, since the handle appearing/disappearing needs to be visible.
  let sliderWidth =
    Math.min(this.range() + this.HANDLE_WIDTH, xPos + sectionDurationWidth) - Math.max(xPos, -this.HANDLE_WIDTH);

  if (xPos > this.range() || xPos + sectionDurationWidth < 0) {
    sliderWidth = 0;
  }

  this.sliderLeft.set(sliderLeft);
  this.sliderWidth.set(sliderWidth);
}

Clipping the boundary at 0 makes the handle look like it's abruptly cut off at the viewport edge, but starting from -HANDLE_WIDTH instead lets the handle appear to slide in naturally from off-screen. Recording the drag's starting offset (shiftX) — so grabbing any point on the handle and dragging still moves it relative to that grabbed point — is a detail in the same spirit.

12. Calculating Playable Sections — Intersection/Difference of Ranges

Handling the Phase 2 "playable sections" requirement meant computing the intersection between the thumbnail section and the playable sections, then darkening whatever fell outside that (the inactive parts). I solved this with standard interval operations for intersection/difference across lists of ranges.

findIntersection(
  playableSections: VideoEditor.PlayableSection[],
  targetSection: VideoEditor.Section
): VideoEditor.Section[] {
  const result = [];

  for (const playableSection of playableSections) {
    const intersectionStart = Math.max(playableSection.startTimeSec, targetSection.startTimeSec);
    const intersectionEnd = Math.min(playableSection.endTimeSec, targetSection.endTimeSec);

    if (intersectionStart < intersectionEnd) {
      result.push({startTimeSec: intersectionStart, endTimeSec: intersectionEnd});
    }
  }

  return result;
}

Going the other way — subtracting several sections (subtrahends) from a single section (minuend) — is trickier. The branching depends on whether the subtracted section fully covers the target, only overlaps its left/right edge, or cuts through the middle.

subtractSection(minuend: VideoEditor.Section, subtrahends: VideoEditor.Section[]): VideoEditor.Section[] {
  if (subtrahends.length === 0) {
    return [minuend];
  }

  const result: VideoEditor.Section[] = [];

  for (let i = 0; i < subtrahends.length; i++) {
    const subtrahend = subtrahends[i];
    const hasNextSubtrahend = i + 1 < subtrahends.length;
    const hasPrevSubtrahend = i - 1 >= 0;

    if (subtrahend.startTimeSec <= minuend.startTimeSec && subtrahend.endTimeSec >= minuend.endTimeSec) {
      return []; // fully covered
    } else if (subtrahend.startTimeSec <= minuend.startTimeSec && subtrahend.endTimeSec < minuend.endTimeSec) {
      result.push({
        startTimeSec: subtrahend.endTimeSec,
        endTimeSec: hasNextSubtrahend ? Math.min(subtrahends[i + 1].startTimeSec, minuend.endTimeSec) : minuend.endTimeSec,
      });
    } else if (minuend.startTimeSec < subtrahend.startTimeSec && subtrahend.endTimeSec < minuend.endTimeSec) {
      result.push({startTimeSec: minuend.startTimeSec, endTimeSec: subtrahend.startTimeSec});
      result.push({startTimeSec: subtrahend.endTimeSec, endTimeSec: minuend.endTimeSec});
    } else if (minuend.startTimeSec < subtrahend.startTimeSec && minuend.endTimeSec <= subtrahend.endTimeSec) {
      result.push({
        startTimeSec: hasPrevSubtrahend ? Math.max(minuend.startTimeSec, subtrahends[i - 1].endTimeSec) : minuend.startTimeSec,
        endTimeSec: subtrahend.startTimeSec,
      });
    }
  }

  if (result.length === 0) {
    return [minuend];
  }

  return uniqWith(result, isEqual);
}

Based on this result, a semi-transparent black rectangle is painted over the inactive sections on the canvas.

for (const section of nonPlayableSections) {
  thumbnailRailCtx.fillStyle = "rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.4)";
  thumbnailRailCtx.fillRect(
    section.startTimeSec - this.baseCoordinatesX + this.sidePadding(),
    this.TOP_PADDING,
    section.endTimeSec - section.startTimeSec + 1,
    this.THUMBNAIL_HEIGHT,
  );
}

13. Implementing Ellipsis Truncation on Canvas by Hand

Once sections could be split into multiple pieces, the label attached to each section ("Section A", "Section B", ...) also had to be truncated to fit its section's width. In HTML, this would be a one-line text-overflow: ellipsis, but canvas has no such property, so I had to count characters by hand and cut the string myself.

private getEllipsizedText(labelContent: VideoEditor.TimelineLabelContent, maxWidth: number): string {
  const labelRailCtx = this.labelRail()?.nativeElement.getContext('2d');
  ...
  const ellipsis = '...';
  const ellipsisWidth = Math.floor(labelRailCtx.measureText(ellipsis).width);

  if (maxWidth < ellipsisWidth + this.TEXT_SIDE_PADDING * 2) {
    return '';
  }

  let result = '';
  let i = 0;

  for (i; i < labelContent.text.length; i++) {
    const char = labelContent.text[i];

    if (labelRailCtx.measureText(result + char).width + this.TEXT_SIDE_PADDING * 2 > maxWidth) {
      break;
    }

    result += char;
  }

  if (i !== labelContent.text.length) {
    for (let j = labelContent.text.length; j > 0; j--) {
      const textWidth = Math.floor(
        labelRailCtx.measureText(result).width + this.TEXT_SIDE_PADDING * 2 + ellipsisWidth
      );

      if (textWidth <= maxWidth) {
        result += ellipsis;

        break;
      }

      result = result.slice(0, -1);
    }
  }

  return result;
}

It grows the string character by character, measuring width with measureText each time, and stops right before it would exceed maxWidth. If appending "..." at that point still overflows, it trims one more character from the end at a time until it fits (the second loop). If the label isn't even wide enough to fit "..." alone, it returns an empty string and skips drawing text entirely — reproducing, pixel by pixel, what HTML's text-overflow: ellipsis normally gives you for free.

Deciding whether to draw a label at all when its section is only partially visible at the screen's edge was a similar kind of problem.

private checkLabelDisplay(labelContent: VideoEditor.TimelineLabelContent): boolean {
  const labelRail = this.labelRail();
  const xPos = this.getLabelXPos(labelContent);
  const labelWidth = this.getLabelWidth(labelContent);

  if (labelWidth <= 0) {
    return false;
  }

  return (xPos < 0 && xPos + labelWidth >= 0) || (xPos > 0 && xPos < labelRail.nativeElement.offsetWidth);
}

A label is drawn if its right edge still overlaps the viewport even though its left edge is off-screen, and skipped if it's entirely off-screen. The same "element partially visible at the screen boundary" problem we saw with the slider handle shows up again here for labels.

14. Why Splitting a Section Leaves a 1-Second Gap

In an earlier screenshot, splitting a section left the two pieces slightly apart instead of flush against each other — that's not a bug, it's an intentional policy. The moment a split happens, the new section is created like this:

splitPlayableSection(
  playableSections: VideoEditor.PlayableSection[],
  targetTimeSec: number,
  minPlayableSectionDuration: number
): VideoEditor.PlayableSection[] {
  const currentSectionIdx = this.getContainingSectionIdx(playableSections, targetTimeSec);

  if (currentSectionIdx === -1) {
    return [];
  }

  const currentSection = playableSections[currentSectionIdx];

  if (
    targetTimeSec - currentSection.startTimeSec < minPlayableSectionDuration ||
    currentSection.endTimeSec - targetTimeSec < minPlayableSectionDuration
  ) {
    return [];
  }

  // Given [0, 100] [101, 200], there's a 1-second gap between 100 and 101 seconds, but we treat it as [0, 200).
  // That's because the current UI has no way to select 100~101.
  const newSection = {startTimeSec: targetTimeSec + 1, endTimeSec: currentSection.endTimeSec};

  currentSection.endTimeSec = targetTimeSec;

  return this.setIdToPlayableSections([
    ...playableSections.slice(0, currentSectionIdx + 1),
    newSection,
    ...playableSections.slice(currentSectionIdx + 1),
  ]);
}

targetTimeSec itself stays with the preceding section, and the following section starts at targetTimeSec + 1 — meaning the 1 second at the cut point belongs to neither side, left as an "unselectable gap." Since there's no UI to select anything finer than a whole second, leaving this 1-second gap was the only way to guarantee the two sections never share a boundary.

Conversely, if you widen a section again and this gap narrows, there's no reason to keep them as two separate sections, so they get merged back into one.

mergePlayableSections(playableSections: VideoEditor.PlayableSection[]): VideoEditor.PlayableSection[] {
  if (playableSections.length <= 1) {
    return playableSections;
  }

  const sortedSections = playableSections.sort((a, b) => a.startTimeSec - b.startTimeSec);
  const mergedSections = [sortedSections[0]];

  for (let i = 1; i < sortedSections.length; i++) {
    const {startTimeSec: prevStartTimeSec, endTimeSec: prevEndTimeSec} = mergedSections[mergedSections.length - 1];
    const {startTimeSec, endTimeSec} = sortedSections[i];

    // Given [0, 100] [101, 200], there's a 1-second gap between 100 and 101 seconds, but we treat it as [0, 200).
    // That's because the current UI has no way to select 100~101.
    if (prevEndTimeSec + 1 >= startTimeSec) {
      mergedSections[mergedSections.length - 1] = {
        id: mergedSections[mergedSections.length - 1].id,
        startTimeSec: prevStartTimeSec,
        endTimeSec: Math.max(prevEndTimeSec, endTimeSec),
      };
    } else {
      mergedSections.push(sortedSections[i]);
    }
  }

  return mergedSections;
}

Both functions use the same threshold — "a gap of 1 second or less." If the threshold used to create the gap when splitting and the one used to remove it when merging ever drift apart, you get bugs: sections re-merging after only a tiny nudge post-split, or the opposite, two sections that look fully joined but staying stubbornly separate. The identical Korean comment sitting side-by-side in both functions is a trace of keeping that threshold in sync.

Wrap-up

That's a rundown of the issues I ran into building this timeline directly on Canvas, and the fixes I found for each along the way. Broadly, they fell into two buckets — one was "the timing between video decoding and canvas drawing can't be trusted" (the seeked event, assigning currentTime, the duration value), and the other was "the sheer complexity of code that deals with coordinate systems" (scroll coordinates, side padding, handle width, intersection/difference of playable sections, and the boundary values involved in splitting and merging).

title: Reasoning in Real World Clinical Care: Why Large Language Models Are Not Yet Safe for Autonomous Clinical Decision Support
description:
arXiv:2607.28677v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM now pass medical licensing examinations and, in curated cases, can rival physicians at diagnostic reasoning. These developments have accelerated the use of LLMs for symptom assessment and clinical decision support in diagnostic and treatment guidance, administrative documentation, and rules-based alert enhancement. This Perspective concerns the most consequential of these applications: the autonomous triage of self-presenting, undifferentiated patients, with little or no clinician in the loop. For that task, the evidence of safety does not yet exist. The gap is not in medical knowledge but in the fidelity of clinical evaluation: a model optimized to continue the most probable text is not optimized to act safely when the safe answer is the improbable must-not-miss diagnosis. Safe triage is not the selection of the most likely diagnosis; it is a sequential decision under asymmetric cost, in which the single catastrophic miss outweighs many false alarms, and the decisive signal may be one the patient has not volunteered - and that the model has not been trained to seek. The core deficit is therefore one of information gathering under uncertainty. Under incomplete histories, LLM systems may fail to show the behaviors safe triage requires: broadening the differential; seeking the missing red flag; lowering the threshold for escalation; deferring judgement until sufficient information is obtained; and escalating concern where high-harm diagnoses remain unexcluded. These modes of failure for LLMs can be difficult to detect considering that evaluations to date often use complete, well-curated, confidence-gated simulations. The application of LLMs under these conditions may be amplified by assistant-like behaviors and positive bias, including credulity, agreeableness, and miscalibration - when these are not constrained by clinical triage logic.

title: CorrelationFlow: A Training-Free Geometric Approach for LiDAR Scene Flow Estimation
description:
arXiv:2607.29237v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LiDAR scene flow estimation has settled into a monoculture: nearly all recent methods share the same feed-forward architecture and the same family of self-supervised losses, inheriting each other's assumptions, and each other's blind spots. When those assumptions fail, as they do for sparse, distant, or fast-moving objects, every method built on them fails together, and adding parameters or simulated training data does not fix what the formulation itself gets wrong. This paper takes the opposite path. We present CorrelationFlow, a training-free geometric framework that reduces scene flow to two textbook operations: connected-component labeling and correlation maximization on bird's-eye-view occupancy images. Objects are isolated as spatio-temporal connected components, their motions recovered as correlation peaks, and the resulting velocities propagated to all member points. However, this dense correlation evaluates every candidate displacement of every cluster and requires a window of past sweeps; therefore, we develop a sparse counterpart that operates on a single sweep pair by matching lightweight occupancy descriptors at boundary key points. Because nothing is trained, nothing is inherited: on the multi-domain test set of the Argoverse 2 2026 Scene Flow Challenge, spanning five datasets with heterogeneous sensors and platforms, CorrelationFlow ranked second among unsupervised methods and degrades most gracefully at long range, where the shared assumptions of learned methods break down. Our results suggest that a substantial share of the scene flow problem is solvable by classical computer vision, and that progress may require questioning the formulation, not scaling it.

title: Representations from Pretrained Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials as Coarse Coordinates for Material Generation and Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2607.28776v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative machine learning is increasingly used for inorganic crystal structure generation. Most models and the corresponding evaluation approaches rely on simple forms of crystal structure representation. In this paper, we showcase the power of atom-averaged features from pretrained Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs), such as MACE, for such tasks. We first introduce a distance measure that assesses the output of material generative models by capturing both quality and novelty in a single distribution-based evaluation framework. In particular, we introduce the Coarse-Fine Transport Distance (CFTD) using two different featurizers, where the quality component is based on coarse MACE features. We showcase CFTD's versatility in capturing crystal-structure quality while also detecting memorization, and compare it with the recently introduced continuous SUN metrics. We further show that coarse MACE features can be used as guidance for a material generative model.

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

import {
  useGetMyApplicationsQuery,
} from "../services/applicationApi";

const PAGE_SIZE = 6;

const useMyApplications = () => {
  // ==========================================
  // PAGINATION
  // ==========================================
  const [pageNumber, setPageNumber] = useState(1);

  // ==========================================
  // SEARCH
  // ==========================================
  const [searchInput, setSearchInput] = useState("");
  const [searchTerm, setSearchTerm] = useState("");

  // ==========================================
  // STATUS FILTER
  // ==========================================
  const [statusFilter, setStatusFilter] = useState("");

  // ==========================================
  // SEARCH DEBOUNCE
  // ==========================================
  useEffect(() => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => {
      setPageNumber(1);
      setSearchTerm(searchInput);
    }, 500);

    return () => {
      clearTimeout(timer);
    };
  }, [searchInput]);

  // ==========================================
  // GET APPLICATIONS
  // ==========================================
  const {
    data,
    isLoading,
    isFetching,
    isError,
  } = useGetMyApplicationsQuery({
    pageSize: PAGE_SIZE,
    pageNumber,
    searchTerm,
    statusFilter,
  });

  // ==========================================
  // APPLICATION DATA
  // ==========================================
  const applications = data?.data ?? [];

  const totalPages = data?.totalPages ?? 1;

  // ==========================================
  // SEARCH
  // ==========================================
  const handleSearch = (value: string) => {
    setSearchInput(value);
  };

  // ==========================================
  // STATUS FILTER
  // ==========================================
  const handleStatusChange = (value: string) => {
    setStatusFilter(value);
    setPageNumber(1);
  };

  // ==========================================
  // PREVIOUS PAGE
  // ==========================================
  const handlePreviousPage = () => {
    if (pageNumber > 1 && !isFetching) {
      setPageNumber((previousPage) => previousPage - 1);
    }
  };

  // ==========================================
  // NEXT PAGE
  // ==========================================
  const handleNextPage = () => {
    if (pageNumber < totalPages && !isFetching) {
      setPageNumber((previousPage) => previousPage + 1);
    }
  };

  return {
    applications,

    pageNumber,
    totalPages,

    searchInput,
    statusFilter,

    isLoading,
    isFetching,
    isError,

    handleSearch,
    handleStatusChange,
    handlePreviousPage,
    handleNextPage,
  };
};

export default useMyApplications;

  // ==========================================

  const [withdrawingApplicationId, setWithdrawingApplicationId] =
    useState<number | null>(null);

  // ==========================================

      case "applied":
        return "bg-blue-100 text-blue-700";

        return "bg-yellow-100 text-yellow-700";

      case "approved":

        return "bg-red-100 text-red-700";

        return "bg-purple-100 text-purple-700";

      default:

    }
  };

  // ==========================================
  // WITHDRAW APPLICATION
  // ==========================================

  const handleWithdraw = async (applicationId: number) => {

      await withdraw(applicationId);

      setWithdrawingApplicationId(null);

  // ==========================================

  // ==========================================

          Track your property applications and their status.

      </div>

      {/* ========================================
          SEARCH & FILTER
      ======================================== */}

      <div className="mb-6 flex flex-col gap-3 sm:flex-row">
        {/* SEARCH */}

        <div className="w-full sm:max-w-md">
          <input
            type="text"
            value={searchInput}
            onChange={(e) => {
              handleSearch(e.target.value);
            }}
            placeholder="Search property or agency..."
            className="
              w-full
              rounded-lg
              border border-gray-300
              bg-white
              px-4 py-3
              text-gray-900
              outline-none
              transition
              focus:border-blue-500
              focus:ring-2
              focus:ring-blue-200
            "
          />
        </div>

        {/* STATUS FILTER */}

        <select
          value={statusFilter}
          onChange={(e) => {
            handleStatusChange(e.target.value);
          }}
          className="
            rounded-lg
            border border-gray-300
            bg-white
            px-4 py-3
            text-gray-700
            outline-none
            transition
            focus:border-blue-500
            focus:ring-2
            focus:ring-blue-200
          "
        >
          <option value="">All Status</option>

          <option value="Applied">Applied</option>

          <option value="Shortlisted">Shortlisted</option>

          <option value="Rejected">Rejected</option>

          <option value="Approved">Approved</option>

          <option value="Leased">Leased</option>
        </select>
      </div>

      {/* ========================================
          FETCHING INDICATOR
      ======================================== */}

      {isFetching && (
        <p className="mb-4 text-sm text-blue-600">
          Updating applications...
        </p>
      )}

      {/* ========================================
          APPLICATION CARDS
      ======================================== */}

      {applications.length === 0 ? (
        <div
          className="
            rounded-xl
            border border-gray-200
            bg-white
            p-10
            text-center
          "
        >
          <p className="text-gray-600">
            No applications found.
          </p>
        </div>
      ) : (
        <div
          className="
            grid
            grid-cols-1
            gap-5
            md:grid-cols-2
            xl:grid-cols-3
          "
        >
          {applications.map((application) => {

            return (
              <div

                  flex
                  flex-col
                  rounded-2xl
                  border border-gray-200
                  bg-white
                  p-5
                  shadow-sm
                  transition
                  duration-200
                  hover:-translate-y-1
                  hover:shadow-lg
                "
              >
                {/* ==================================
                    CARD HEADER

                <div
                  className="
                    flex

                    justify-between
                    gap-3
                  "
                >
                  <div className="min-w-0">

                        text-gray-900

                      py-1
                      text-xs
                      font-semibold
                      ${getStatusStyle(application.status)}
                    `}
                  >
                    {application.status}
                  </span>
                </div>

                {/* ==================================
                    CARD DETAILS
                ================================== */}

                <div className="mt-5 space-y-4">
                  {/* LOCATION */}

                  <div>
                    <p className="text-xs text-gray-400">
                      Property Location
                    </p>

                    <p className="mt-1 text-sm font-medium text-gray-800">
                      {application.propertyLocation}
                    </p>
                  </div>

                  {/* APPLIED DATE */}

                  <div>
                    <p className="text-xs text-gray-400">
                      Applied Date
                    </p>

                    <p className="mt-1 text-sm font-medium text-gray-800">
                      {new Date(
                        application.appliedOn
                      ).toLocaleDateString("en-IN")}
                    </p>
                  </div>

                  {/* MOVE IN DATE */}

                  <div>
                    <p className="text-xs text-gray-400">
                      Move-in Date
                    </p>

                    <p className="mt-1 text-sm font-medium text-gray-800">
                      {new Date(
                        application.moveInDate
                      ).toLocaleDateString("en-IN")}
                    </p>
                  </div>

                  {/* LEASE DURATION */}

                  <div>
                    <p className="text-xs text-gray-400">
                      Lease Duration
                    </p>

                    <p className="mt-1 text-sm font-medium text-gray-800">
                      {application.leaseDuration} months
                    </p>
                  </div>
                </div>

                {/* ==================================
                    ACTION BUTTONS
                ================================== */}

                <div
                  className="
                    mt-auto
                    flex
                    gap-3
                    border-t
                    border-gray-100
                    pt-5
                  "
                >
                  {/* VIEW DETAILS */}

                  <button
                    type="button"
                    className="
                      flex
                      flex-1
                      items-center
                      justify-center
                      gap-2
                      rounded-lg
                      border
                      border-blue-500
                      px-3
                      py-2
                      text-sm
                      font-medium
                      text-blue-600
                      transition
                      hover:bg-blue-50
                    "

                    <FaEye size={14} />

                  {/* WITHDRAW */}

                  <button
                    type="button"
                    disabled={
                      application.isWithDraw ||
                      isWithdrawing
                    }
                    onClick={() =>
                      handleWithdraw(application.id)
                    }
                    className="
                      flex
                      flex-1
                      items-center
                      justify-center
                      gap-2
                      rounded-lg
                      bg-gray-900
                      px-3
                      py-2
                      text-sm
                      font-medium
                      text-white
                      transition
                      hover:bg-gray-800
                      disabled:cursor-not-allowed
                      disabled:opacity-50
                    "
                  >
                    <FaUndo size={14} />

                    {isCurrentApplicationWithdrawing
                      ? "Withdrawing..."
                      : application.isWithDraw
                        ? "Withdrawn"
                        : "Withdraw"}
                  </button>
                </div>
              </div>
            );
          })}
        </div>
      )}

      {/* ========================================
          PAGINATION
      ======================================== */}

      <div
        className="
          mt-6
          flex
          flex-col
          gap-3
          border-t
          border-gray-200
          pt-5
          sm:flex-row
          sm:items-center
          sm:justify-between
        "
      >
        {/* PAGE INFO */}

        <p className="text-sm text-gray-600">
          Page{" "}
          <span className="font-semibold text-gray-900">
            {pageNumber}
          </span>{" "}
          of{" "}
          <span className="font-semibold text-gray-900">
            {totalPages}
          </span>
        </p>

        {/* PAGINATION BUTTONS */}

        <div className="flex gap-2">
          {/* PREVIOUS */}

          <button
            type="button"
            disabled={
              pageNumber === 1 ||
              isFetching
            }
            onClick={handlePreviousPage}
            className="
              rounded-lg
              border border-gray-300
              bg-white
              px-4 py-2
              text-sm
              font-medium
              text-gray-700
              transition
              hover:bg-gray-100
              disabled:cursor-not-allowed
              disabled:opacity-50
            "
          >
            Previous
          </button>

          {/* NEXT */}

          <button
            type="button"
            disabled={
              pageNumber >= totalPages ||
              isFetching
            }
            onClick={handleNextPage}
            className="
              rounded-lg
              border border-gray-300
              bg-white
              px-4 py-2
              text-sm
              font-medium
              text-gray-700
              transition
              hover:bg-gray-100
              disabled:cursor-not-allowed
              disabled:opacity-50
            "
          >
            Next
          </button>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
};

title: I built a page that only publishes numbers surviving our own checks. It caught me inside the hour.
description:
I run a verified inference endpoint. What we sell is checking: we verify results before serving them, and we say so when we cannot.

Every claim defect we shipped this month had the same shape. A number was measured honestly, the configuration underneath it changed, and the number stayed on the page. Our benchmark rows were measured on model tiers we retired weeks earlier. Nothing was fabricated. Everything was stale.

So I built a page that cannot go stale. It is generated from the live gateway config, and every badge on it is derived rather than written. If a measurement's configuration premise no longer matches what is running, the page strikes the number and says why.

It went live. Within the hour it caught me publishing two numbers our own ledger explicitly withholds.

What the page does

For each path through the system it states four things:

  1. What "good" means on that path, and whether a real oracle checked it. Tool calls are checked against the schema. Code runs against your tests in a sandbox. Free prose gets nothing, because there is nothing to run.
  2. The measurement, with n, interval and date.
  3. Whether that measurement still describes the running system, graded automatically against live config.
  4. Whether it passed adversarial review, and if not, that appears on the page next to the number.

The third item is the whole point. A number and a config are two facts that drift apart silently, and no amount of care fixes that. A generator that reads both cannot lie about the gap.

The catch

I put our tool-calling and trap-set results on it. Both are good numbers. Both are marked in our internal claims ledger as not cleared for external citation, owes adversarial verify.

I had written the page whose entire purpose is publishing only what survives our checks, and I had not run the check.

The first fix was a blocklist for that one phrase. Also wrong. Our ledger withholds rows in at least six phrasings, and a blocklist misses the seventh. For a public claim the gate has to fail closed: a figure publishes only if its ledger row exists and carries no hold marker. Over-withholding costs a number on a page. Under-withholding costs a retraction.

Failing closed immediately caught two more, subtler ones. Two figures had no ledger row at all, because I had sourced them from an internal handoff instead of the truth layer. One was a 30/40 result. Our ledger also contains a 30/40, from a completely different run on a different model. Same number, different measurement. That is exactly the confusion an uncited figure invites.

Then the reviewer rejected my draft

The remaining claim needed real adversarial review, so I commissioned one and briefed it to refute rather than agree. It came back do not publish, with three specific defects:

  • I wrote that our agreement gate accepts a wrong answer "roughly a quarter to a third of the time." That range was two underpowered subgroups (6 of 25, and 5 of 15) whose confidence intervals almost entirely overlap. It reads like a stable operating characteristic. The data supports one pooled binomial: 11 of 40, 27.5%, Wilson 95% interval 16.1 to 42.8.
  • I quoted "1.7 to 3.5% on code." It has the shape of a measured interval. The reviewer said the evidence was not in my brief, which would normally mean I under-briefed it. So I checked instead of accepting. The figure appears three times in our ledger with no n, no interval and no date anywhere. The gap was real.
  • I wrote "near zero on arithmetic." That is residue from a claim we retracted publicly after a reader caught it from our own article's text. No clean replacement exists, so the phrase cannot appear at all.

I took all three. I refused one instruction: it wanted me to name an internal threshold, which is recipe rather than result. It did not know that because I had not briefed it on our disclosure policy. Same failure, other direction.

The green check that could not fail

While extending our claims gate to cover more surfaces, I did something I should have done when it was written: I injected the defect it exists to catch.

Seven injections. Five wrong percentages, a struck cost multiple, a retracted compounding claim. It fired on none of them. Its tolerance covers most of the range it checks, so almost any number is "backed" by something. It had been printing OK every morning for weeks.

It was not lying. Its own output says "values checked, not claims," and a comment in its source says the same. The defect is one level out: a green line on a status board is read as protection, and nobody re-reads the caveat.

A guard you have never watched fail is not a guard. It is a habit.

The rules that transfer

A correction in your repo is not a correction in public. Our live site was still serving retracted figures while every internal instrument reported the sweep as done, because every internal instrument greps the repo. Verify a public claim by fetching the public URL.

Your measurement tool is an instrument, so verify it first. Our cost script summed one of three cost columns. It reported one cent where the truth was $1.73, and it was the exact script our ledger's cost row cited.

A readability filter can eat an error. I piped a remote script through grep -v to hide a deprecation warning. A database auth failure exited zero, and that became STATUS: Success, then a fleet-wide OK across both production boxes. The lie got more authoritative at every hop.

Placeholders are claims. Our dashboard rendered "$1,284 saved this month" as static HTML before live data arrived. A brand-new account with zero usage would have been shown a fabricated saving. I found it while opening signup to the public, one step before strangers would have seen it.

Publish the path where you are weaker. Our trap set is 200 of 200 on the primary path. Under failover it is 30 of 40, and every miss is the same verdict: it calls a tool where it should decline. Both numbers are on the page. The second is the more useful one.

Go and check it

The page is live at tirtha.ai/capabilities. Seven paths, what checks each one, what it measured, and the review state of every figure.

To try it rather than read about it, tirtha.ai/verify runs live against our API with no key and no signup. Three prefilled adversarial cases, and you can watch it decline a call instead of inventing one.

To run it on your own workload: go to tirtha.ai, click Get an API key, sign in with Google, and start. Free while we are in beta. No card, no email, no sales call. You get 100 requests a month and it stops rather than surprises you.

If you find a claim on that page that does not survive, I want to hear it. That is not rhetorical. The last time someone did, they were reading our own published text, and they were right.

title: WebSocket Tick Stream Implementation to Build Complete US Stock Time Series
description:
Intro: The Hidden Time-Series Bias That Skews Institutional Backtests

As quantitative researchers and backend engineers working within asset management teams, our day-to-day work centers on building robust backtesting frameworks and real-time market monitoring pipelines for US equities. We’ve run into a recurring, hard-to-trace bug across multiple internal projects: identical trading algorithms deliver wildly inconsistent performance metrics when fed data from different market sources.
After rounds of comparative backtesting and log auditing, we ruled out flawed candlestick aggregation functions as the root issue. Instead, the discrepancy stems from inconsistent handling rules for pre-market, regular session, and after-hours tick data. Most junior engineers overlook session boundary standardization, which quietly warps price distributions and undermines the credibility of all downstream strategy analysis.

The Structural Differences Between US Stock Trading Sessions

Unlike most single-session equity markets, US equities trade across three distinct daily windows, each with unique liquidity profiles and sensitivity to market news events.
Pre-market: 04:00–09:30 ET, thin order book depth; overnight news and preliminary earnings often trigger sharp, unbalanced price moves
Regular trading hours: 09:30–16:00 ET, peak institutional liquidity; all classic technical indicators are calibrated against this window
After-hours: 16:00–20:00 ET, dominated by post-market earnings releases, prone to rapid short-term volatility

Nearly all modern market data APIs return full tick records covering all three windows, yet many pipelines filter out extended-hour data by default. For example, a stock could rally from $100 to $103 during pre-market. If your code discards those ticks, the opening candle of the regular session will still start near $100. This barely impacts casual chart viewing, but it fundamentally distorts datasets used for factor research, indicator calibration, and multi-year backtesting.

Standard Timestamp Normalization: The Core ETL Foundation

Before aggregating any ticks into candlesticks, we enforce universal timestamp normalization across both offline historical datasets and live streaming feeds. There is no universal aggregation formula for extended-hour data—processing logic must be customized for your business use case.
Our team follows a fixed, reusable ETL pipeline for all US equity tick processing:

Consume raw tick payloads from market APIs
Parse raw millisecond Unix timestamps
Convert timestamps to Eastern Time zone
Tag each tick with its corresponding trading session
Aggregate tagged records into OHLC candlesticks on demand
Time zone alignment is the most error-prone step here. US market rules are governed by America/New_York time, but cloud servers store timestamps in UTC to avoid regional bias. If you render candlesticks directly using raw server timestamps, daylight saving time shifts will introduce permanent 1-hour offsets. Our production standard: persist all raw ticks as UTC timestamps; convert to ET only during session tagging and candlestick rendering.

Custom Candlestick Aggregation Rules Per Workflow

Blindly mixing low-liquidity extended-hour ticks with high-volume regular session prints pollutes volume-based indicators like volume moving averages and turnover ratios. We maintain four standardized processing templates for different research workflows:

Long-term multi-year trend analysis
Only aggregate regular-hours ticks into candlesticks. Pre/after-hour data is archived in separate tables and excluded from indicator calculations, matching the design intent of traditional technical analysis tools.

Intraday & high-frequency strategy backtesting
Include every tick across pre, regular, and after-hours sessions to reconstruct the full daily price trajectory, fully capturing overnight gap risk.

Real-time live market dashboards
Retain unfiltered raw tick streams with no early aggregation to support sub-second visualization.

Earnings event research
Isolate after-hours tick data into independent datasets to avoid signal contamination from intraday trading activity.

Live Tick Stream Integration Using

To eliminate mismatched logic between offline historical data and real-time feeds, we reuse the exact timezone and session tagging functions across both pipelines.
For live US equity tick ingestion, our production stack leverages AllTick API’s persistent WebSocket subscription endpoint to maintain consistent data standards end-to-end.
Below is a minimal working Python snippet for real-time tick subscription and timestamp conversion:

import websocket
import json
from datetime import datetime
import pytz

UTC_ZONE = pytz.utc
NY_ZONE = pytz.timezone("America/New_York")

def tick_receive(ws, raw_data):
    data = json.loads(raw_data)
    symbol = data.get("symbol")
    price = float(data.get("price"))
    ts_ms = data.get("timestamp")
    utc_dt = datetime.fromtimestamp(ts_ms / 1000, tz=UTC_ZONE)
    ny_dt = utc_dt.astimezone(NY_ZONE)
    print(f"Ticker:{symbol} Price:{price} NY Time:{ny_dt}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ws_client = websocket.WebSocketApp(
        "wss://api.alltick.co/stock/websocket",
        on_message=tick_receive
    )
    ws_client.run_forever()

Frequently Overlooked Edge Cases That Break Candlestick Integrity

After deploying dozens of institutional-grade backtesting pipelines, we’ve documented three common hidden pitfalls:

Cross-midnight trading day labeling
Most APIs return timestamps in UTC, while US trading days are defined by Eastern Time. Ticks crossing UTC midnight need date correction to avoid misassigned daily candlestick blocks.

Extended-hour data API parameters
Many market endpoints only return regular session ticks by default. You must explicitly enable extended-hour request flags to retrieve pre/after prints, otherwise gap volatility data will be permanently missing.
Streaming fault tolerance

Production WebSocket pipelines must implement auto-reconnection, duplicate tick deduplication, and timestamp sorting. Unsorted or duplicate ticks generate malformed, unreliable candlestick charts.

Closing Takeaways For Quant & Data Engineers

From an institutional quantitative development perspective, market data APIs are far more than simple price fetching tools. Their true value hinges on your ability to correctly interpret session-based time logic baked into US equity market rules.

There is no one-size-fits-all method to merge pre-market and after-hours ticks. Always design aggregation logic aligned with your research or trading objectives. We recommend finalizing trading session tagging and timestamp normalization rules before writing any candlestick generation code. Standardized time-series preprocessing creates reproducible indicator outputs and reduces performance drift between backtest simulations and live market execution.

title: What Is Missing in Surgical Risk Stratification and Outcome Prediction: A Scoping Review of End-to-End Machine Learning Approaches
description:
arXiv:2607.29090v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Postoperative adverse events, including mortality and morbidity, remain a major global burden, many of which are preventable through early identification of high-risk patients and targeted perioperative care. Accurate risk stratification is therefore essential. With the growing availability of large-scale electronic health records (EHRs), machine learning (ML) provides a data-driven approach to model complex clinical patterns. However, existing studies vary widely in design, and methodological practices remain fragmented. This scoping review characterizes ML pipelines for surgical risk stratification and outcome prediction using EHR data. We reviewed 190 studies covering the ML workflow, including data preprocessing, algorithm selection, model evaluation, and explainability. Most studies relied on single-center private datasets with limited data modalities, while the scarcity of open-access surgical datasets constrained reproducibility and generalizability. Reporting of key preprocessing steps, including missing data handling, feature selection, and class imbalance, was often incomplete. Conventional ML models and simple neural networks predominated, whereas deep learning and multimodal approaches remained uncommon. Benchmark datasets and standardized evaluation protocols were largely absent, hindering cross-study comparisons. Only about one-third of studies incorporated explainability methods. This review identifies methodological gaps limiting clinically robust postoperative ML tools and provides a structured reference to support more rigorous, reproducible, and clinically meaningful ML development for perioperative care.

title: The Death of the Static UI: Building Context-Aware Mobile Apps in 2026
description:
Every app you've ever shipped made the same quiet assumption: the interface is a fixed thing. You design a screen, you lay out the widgets, and every user sees the same arrangement in the same order — a 22-year-old on a commuter train at 8am and a 60-year-old at home on a Sunday get pixel-identical layouts. For thirty years that was simply what a UI was.

That assumption is dying. In 2026 the leading mobile apps treat the interface as a live surface that reshapes itself in real time — reordering navigation, resizing touch targets, shifting color and density, surfacing the one action you're most likely to want next — driven by on-device signals about who you are, where you are, and what you're doing right now. The static screen is becoming the exception, not the default.

Here's what's actually driving it, what it takes to build, and what it looks like in code — with Flutter examples throughout.

From static layout to living surface

The old personalization playbook was recommendation, not adaptation. Netflix reordered a content row; Spotify built you a playlist. The chrome around those recommendations — the navigation, the layout, the visual system — stayed frozen. Context-aware UX pushes personalization down into the interface itself.

Concretely, an adaptive UI reacts to signals like these:

  • Motion and activity — accelerometer and gyroscope tell you the user is walking, driving, or still. A UI can enlarge touch targets and simplify layout when it detects movement, cutting mis-taps.
  • Location and environment — outdoors in bright light, boost contrast and switch to a high-legibility mode; on a known Wi-Fi network at home, load richer media.
  • Time and calendar — automatic dark mode at night, a "leaving for a meeting" layout when the next calendar event is 15 minutes out.
  • Usage history — promote the three features this user actually touches, demote the ones they never open. A finance app foregrounds "transfer" for a power user and "check balance" for a casual one.
  • Device and network state — drop to a minimalist, low-power layout on a dying battery or a weak connection.

The through-line is if/then UX logic: the interface has conditional branches, and an on-device model decides which branch to render.

What it looks like in the wild

These aren't hypotheticals. A few patterns already shipping:

Spotify reshapes its home surface by daypart and activity — a running-friendly, low-interaction layout with big targets and workout playlists surfaces in the morning, while an evening browse session gets denser, discovery-heavy shelves. The context (time, motion, listening history) reorders the screen, not just the recommendations inside it.

Starbucks drives its app home screen with a real-time decision engine that factors in time of day, weather, store location, and past orders — a cold-brew card on a hot afternoon near a store you frequent, a "reorder your usual" button when you're on your commute route. The same app renders materially different first screens to different users in different moments.

Banking apps increasingly reorder the dashboard by learned behavior: a user who checks balances and nothing else gets balance-first, while someone who transfers money weekly gets "transfer" promoted to the top action. Same binary, two different information architectures.

Fitness apps modify the dashboard layout based on workout frequency and current activity state — surfacing "start workout" and simplifying the interface when the accelerometer says you're moving, then switching to progress charts and history when you're stationary.

The unifying idea: the interface is a function of context, computed fresh, on the device.

Why Flutter is a natural fit

Flutter's core model is UI = f(state) — widgets rebuild whenever the state they depend on changes. Context-aware UX is just that idea with the state coming from sensors and a model instead of only user taps. You don't need a new paradigm; you point your existing reactive plumbing (StreamBuilder, ValueListenableBuilder, Riverpod, Bloc — pick your poison) at a stream of context and let the widget tree recompute. And because a single Flutter codebase renders on both platforms, one adaptation layer covers Android and iOS at once.

The platforms underneath are pushing the same direction. Android's Material You 3.0 (with Android 16) extracts 20+ semantic color roles on-device — Flutter taps that dynamic palette through the dynamic_color package, so your theme can follow the system's context-derived colors rather than a hardcoded scheme.

Here's dynamic, context-driven theming in Flutter — the ThemeData itself becomes a function of context:

class AdaptiveApp extends StatelessWidget {
  final UiContext ctx;
  const AdaptiveApp({super.key, required this.ctx});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // dynamic_color surfaces Material You palettes from the OS
    return DynamicColorBuilder(
      builder: (ColorScheme? lightDynamic, ColorScheme? darkDynamic) {
        final useDark = ctx.isNight || ctx.batterySaver;

        var scheme = useDark
            ? (darkDynamic ??
                ColorScheme.fromSeed(
                    seedColor: Colors.teal, brightness: Brightness.dark))
            : (lightDynamic ?? ColorScheme.fromSeed(seedColor: Colors.teal));

        // Nudge toward higher contrast outdoors / in bright light
        if (ctx.ambientLux > 10000) scheme = scheme.toHighContrast();

        return MaterialApp(
          theme: ThemeData(
            colorScheme: scheme,
            // Larger, more legible type when the user is moving
            textTheme: ctx.isMoving ? largeTextTheme : defaultTextTheme,
          ),
          home: HomeScreen(engine: context.read<ContextEngine>()),
        );
      },
    );
  }
}

The engine: on-device ML

Context-aware UX only works because the inference runs locally. You cannot round-trip to a server to decide whether to enlarge a button while someone is walking — the latency kills it, and shipping motion, location, and camera data to the cloud is a privacy non-starter.

The Flutter on-device stack is mature. For the model layer you've got tflite_flutter (Dart bindings to TensorFlow Lite / LiteRT) and the google_mlkit_* packages for ready-made vision and language tasks; on iOS you can bridge to Core ML through a platform channel when you need it. For signals, sensors_plus gives you accelerometer/gyroscope, light reads ambient lux on Android, battery_plus covers power state, and geolocator handles location. The same three-stage pattern maps cleanly onto native Compose/SwiftUI too, if you ever go platform-specific.

A clean pipeline has three stages: a signal-collection layer that samples sensors, system state, and interaction history; an on-device inference layer that turns those raw signals into a prediction; and an adaptation layer that maps the prediction onto concrete UI state.

📷 UPLOAD IMAGE HERE via the toolbar image button — images/context-aware-ux-pipeline.png (the three-stage pipeline diagram)

Stages one and two — collect signals, run a local model, expose the result as a stream the UI can react to:

enum Intent { quickAction, browse }

class UiContext {
  final bool isNight;
  final bool isMoving;
  final double ambientLux;
  final bool batterySaver;
  final Intent predictedIntent; // model output

  const UiContext({
    required this.isNight,
    required this.isMoving,
    required this.ambientLux,
    required this.batterySaver,
    required this.predictedIntent,
  });

  factory UiContext.defaults() => const UiContext(
        isNight: false, isMoving: false, ambientLux: 300,
        batterySaver: false, predictedIntent: Intent.browse);
}

class ContextEngine {
  final SensorHub sensors;
  final Interpreter interpreter; // tflite_flutter

  ContextEngine(this.sensors, this.interpreter);

  // combineLatest4 comes from rxdart
  Stream<UiContext> get context => Rx.combineLatest4(
        sensors.activity,      // walking / still / driving
        sensors.ambientLight,
        sensors.batteryState,
        sensors.usageHistory,
        (Activity activity, double lux, BatteryState battery, Usage usage) {
          final features = featurize(activity, lux, battery, usage, DateTime.now());
          final intent = _runInference(features); // <1ms on-device
          return UiContext(
            isNight: _isNight(DateTime.now()),
            isMoving: activity != Activity.still,
            ambientLux: lux,
            batterySaver: battery.saverOn,
            predictedIntent: intent,
          );
        },
      );

  Intent _runInference(List<double> features) {
    final output = List.filled(Intent.values.length, 0.0)
        .reshape([1, Intent.values.length]);
    interpreter.run([features], output); // on-device, no network
    return Intent.values[_argmax(output[0] as List<double>)];
  }
}

Stage three — the widget tree is a pure function of that context. Because Flutter rebuilds on stream emissions, the screen literally rearranges itself when the prediction flips:

class HomeScreen extends StatelessWidget {
  final ContextEngine engine;
  const HomeScreen({super.key, required this.engine});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return StreamBuilder<UiContext>(
      stream: engine.context,
      initialData: UiContext.defaults(),
      builder: (context, snapshot) {
        final ctx = snapshot.data!;
        final actions = adaptiveActions(ctx.predictedIntent);

        if (ctx.predictedIntent == Intent.quickAction) {
          // Moving / in a hurry: one big primary action, minimal chrome
          return PrimaryActionCard(
            key: const Key('primaryActionCard'),
            action: actions.first,
            size: ctx.isMoving ? CardSize.large : CardSize.medium,
          );
        }
        // Browsing: richer, denser discovery layout
        return DiscoveryGrid(key: const Key('discoveryGrid'), actions: actions);
      },
    );
  }
}

Keep the model small and quantized, sample sensors at the lowest rate that still feels responsive, and gate expensive work on battery and thermal state — an adaptive UI that drains the phone defeats its own purpose. In Flutter, push the interpreter.run call onto a background isolate (via compute or a long-lived isolate) if your model is heavy enough to jank the frame.

A worked example: the commuter's transit app

📷 UPLOAD IMAGE HERE via the toolbar image button — images/context-aware-ux-before-after.png (before/after of the same transit app)

Put the pieces together with one concrete flow. A user opens your transit app at 8:12am on a weekday.

The signal layer reports: activity = walking, time = weekday morning, location = within 200m of their usual station, battery = 34%, usage history = "buys a single-ride ticket most weekday mornings." The inference layer featurizes that and predicts Intent.quickAction with high confidence. The adaptation layer renders a stripped-down screen: a single large "Buy morning ticket — Station A → Downtown" button with a big touch target sized for a walking user, high-contrast colors because ambient light is high, and a dimmed, battery-aware theme. Live departure times sit right below; the trip planner, settings, and promotions collapse behind a menu.

Same user, same app, 7:40pm, sitting at home on Wi-Fi with the phone charging: activity = still, low ambient light, no imminent commute pattern. Now the model predicts Intent.browse, and the screen renders the full discovery layout — trip planner up front, weekend passes, service alerts, a denser dark-mode interface. Two completely different first screens from one code path, decided on-device in under a millisecond, with no user data leaving the phone.

Privacy is what makes it acceptable

The reason this is happening now rather than in 2020 is that the privacy story finally holds up. Users have made clear they'll walk away from apps that feel invasive — surveys this year found a majority lose loyalty to brands that "reduce them to statistics." An architecture that ships behavioral data to a server to personalize is exactly the thing they're rejecting.

On-device inference flips that. The sensitive signals — location, motion, front-camera emotion cues, usage patterns — never leave the device; only the outcome (a rearranged layout) is visible. Where you do need to improve models across your user base, federated learning lets you train on-device and share only gradient updates, and differential privacy adds calibrated noise so no individual's data can be reconstructed from those updates. That combination — local inference plus privacy-preserving training — is what lets you personalize deeply without building a surveillance liability. Treat it as a feature you can market, not a compliance checkbox.

The hard part: your UI is now non-deterministic

Here's the challenge teams underestimate. The moment your interface adapts, you've given up the thing that made mobile QA tractable: a fixed set of screens. There is no single "home screen" to design-review or golden-file test anymore — there's a distribution of home screens, one per context.

The practical fix is to make context an injectable input so you can pin it in tests. Notice that HomeScreen above takes its context from a stream — in a widget test you feed it a fabricated UiContext and assert the resulting layout:

testWidgets('moving commuter gets the quick action', (tester) async {
  const ctx = UiContext(
    isNight: false,
    isMoving: true,
    ambientLux: 12000,
    batterySaver: true,
    predictedIntent: Intent.quickAction,
  );

  await tester.pumpWidget(
    MaterialApp(home: HomeScreen(engine: FakeEngine(ctx))),
  );
  await tester.pump(); // let the stream emit

  expect(find.byKey(const Key('primaryActionCard')), findsOneWidget);
  expect(find.byKey(const Key('discoveryGrid')), findsNothing);
});

That reframes the rest of the discipline too. Design review shifts from approving a comp to approving rules and bounds — designers specify how far the UI is allowed to move, not one frozen state. Accessibility can actually improve here — real-time touch-target enlargement and automatic WCAG-compliant contrast are natural fits for adaptive systems — but only if you make it an explicit adaptation rule rather than hoping it falls out.

And you have to respect a stability budget. A UI that rearranges itself too often is disorienting; users build spatial memory, and moving the button they reach for by reflex is a bug, not a feature. Adapt at sensible boundaries — app launch, a clear context change — not continuously. Over-personalization also risks echo chambers and the creepy-manipulation feeling that erodes trust, so give users a visible, easy way to see and reset how the app has adapted to them.

Why it's worth the complexity

The pull is commercial, and the numbers vendors and analysts cite are large: personalized calls-to-action outperform generic ones by around 200%, extensive personalization has been linked to triple-digit lifts in revenue per user, and a majority of business leaders report higher retention from it. Treat the specific figures as directional — they come from marketing research, not controlled trials — but the direction is consistent and it's why every major platform is now shipping the primitives.

The static screen was always a compromise: one layout that had to be acceptable for everyone and optimal for no one. On-device ML removes the reason for that compromise. The interface can finally meet each user in their actual moment — walking or sitting, morning or midnight, power user or newcomer — without asking them to configure anything or surrendering their data to do it.

The screen that never changes is starting to look like the thing that dates your app. In 2026, the interface is a conversation with context — and the apps that learn to hold that conversation are the ones users stay in.

title: Forwardrobe: Garment-Aware Gaussian Avatars from a Single Image
description:
arXiv:2607.29106v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars from a single image remains particularly challenging for loose garments, whose geometry and motion cannot be adequately represented by body-aligned topology and skinning. We present Forwardrobe, a feed-forward framework for reconstructing garment-aware Gaussian avatars from a single image. Forwardrobe explicitly separates clothing from the body in canonical Gaussian space and equips the garment layer with continuity-aware geometry and skinning initialization, pose-conditioned non-rigid deformation, and appearance adaptation. These designs improve garment reconstruction and visual quality during animation, particularly for skirts and dresses. The separated garment layer additionally forms an independently controllable 3D asset, enabling garment editing, transfer, and 3D virtual try-on. Experiments demonstrate improved garment reconstruction quality and greater flexibility in garment manipulation compared with existing single-image avatar reconstruction methods.

title: EarlyDx: An Admission-Anchored Benchmark for Open-Ended Generation of Evidence-Supported ED-Encounter Diagnoses
description:
arXiv:2607.28788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical diagnosis at hospital admission must be made rapidly from limited, incomplete evidence. Existing diagnosis-prediction benchmarks are poorly suited to this setting: they restrict prediction to closed code sets, exclude free-text notes, and supervise with discharge diagnoses that incorporate the full inpatient course. We introduce EarlyDx, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended early diagnosis, built from 154,834 emergency department encounters in MIMIC-IV. Each encounter is restricted to records available at admission time $t_0$ and supervised by the diagnoses recorded during the ED encounter rather than at discharge. An LLM auditor further verifies every free-text label as supported, partially supported, or unsupported by that evidence; the primary evaluation scores only fully supported labels. Under a semantic LLM-as-judge protocol, no evaluated system --- frontier general, medical-specialized, or in-domain post-trained --- synthesizes admission-time evidence reliably. Zero-shot models score largely by extraction, recovering only 3-31% of diagnoses that must be inferred rather than read from the record; post-training raises inference-dependent recall to 56%, but a sizeable margin remains, and on time-critical conditions no system attains a clinician's balance of sensitivity and precision. We release the full construction and evaluation pipeline at here.

title: Dynamics-aware identification of governing equations from sparse and noisy data
description:
arXiv:2607.29036v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) and PDE functional identification (PDE-FIND) recover parsimonious ordinary and partial differential equations (ODEs and PDEs) from data. However, sparse and noisy temporal measurements can make derivative estimates unreliable. To address this problem, we evaluate Koopman-based upsampling techniques implemented with dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), extended DMD (EDMD), and optimized DMD. These methods learn finite-dimensional approximations of Koopman evolution on selected observables and are used to interpolate and denoise snapshots inside the observed time window before derivative estimation and sparse regression. The empirical benchmark comprises two ODE systems, Lorenz-63 and Van der Pol, and three periodic PDE systems, Burgers, Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovskii-Piskunov (Fisher-KPP), and linear advection-diffusion, over sparse and noisy sampling regimes. Polynomial EDMD gives the strongest ODE results, especially in coefficient accuracy. The PDE results are system-dependent: low-rank DMD-assisted reconstructions improve Burgers and advection-diffusion discovery, while the raw baseline (without upsampling) remains competitive for the Fisher-KPP data. A comparison against linear and smoothing-spline interpolation techniques shows that the selected Koopman-based preprocessors provide overall performance gains over these non-dynamical alternatives. We also demonstrate that DMD-assisted upsampling can stabilize Pareto-based non-oracle support-size selection. Overall, Koopman-based upsampling is best viewed as a dynamics-aware preprocessing step that can reduce derivative-estimation error when its observable representation and low-rank structure are appropriate for the data.
